passages.t: The first book, and forty days
passages.happening:
Luke begins by speaking to the same man he wrote his Gospel for: “In my first book, O Theophilus, I wrote about all that Jesus began to do and to teach” (verse 1). That first book ran until the day Jesus was taken up to heaven.

Now Luke goes back a step. After Jesus suffered and died, “He presented Himself to them with many convincing proofs that He was alive” (verse 3). He did not appear once and vanish. He showed himself to them again and again, over forty days, and he spoke with them about the kingdom of God.
passages.hearers:
Theophilus was the man Luke wrote both books for. His name means ‘friend of God’. He may have been a patron who paid for the copying of the books, or a believer being taught, and some have wondered if the name stands for every reader who loves God. A real person is the most likely.

Notice the word ‘began’. The Gospel told what Jesus began to do and teach. So Acts is not a new story about the apostles taking over from Jesus. It is the same story going on, with Jesus still at work, now from heaven.

Luke's word for ‘convincing proofs’ means sure signs, the kind of proof that settles a question. Luke wants his reader to know that the first Christians did not believe Jesus was alive because they wished it. They saw him, ate with him and talked with him, many times. The Gospel had already told how he ate a piece of fish in front of them (Luke 24:42-43).
passages.ot:
Forty is a number Scripture uses for times of testing and preparing. Moses stayed on the mountain with God “forty days and forty nights” (Exodus 24:18). Elijah walked “forty days and forty nights” to the mountain of God (1 Kings 19:8). Jesus was tested in the desert for forty days (Luke 4:2). Many readers notice that the forty days after Easter are a time of preparing too: the disciples are being made ready for their work.

The subject of those days was ‘the kingdom of God’. That was the hope of Israel's prophets, the day when God would rule openly, as Daniel saw: “His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed” (Daniel 7:14).
passages.asks: Luke cared that his reader could be sure. Faith in Acts is not a leap in the dark. It rests on what people saw and touched. Ask what you have actually been told about Jesus' rising, and whether you have ever looked at the evidence for yourself. And notice that the risen Jesus spent his last days with his friends teaching them. He did not leave them to guess.

passages.t: Wait for the Spirit; you will be My witnesses
passages.happening:
While they are together, Jesus tells them, “Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift the Father promised” (verse 4). John baptized with water, he says, “but in a few days you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (verse 5).

They ask him a question that has been on their minds: “Lord, will You at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” (verse 6).

Jesus does not answer the question of timing. “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by His own authority” (verse 7). Instead he gives them a promise and a task: “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
‘Baptized with the Holy Spirit’ takes the hearer back to John the Baptist, who had said that one stronger than he was coming, who would baptize “with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Luke 3:16). Jesus now says that promise is about to come true.

The disciples' question was a natural one for Jews of their day. Many hoped God would free Israel from its enemies and set up his kingdom openly, with a king from David's line. The prophets had promised that God would gather his scattered people. Now their Messiah had risen from the dead. Was this the moment?

Verse 8 is the map of the whole book. Jerusalem was the city. Judea was the country around it. Samaria lay to the north, and its people, the Samaritans, worshipped on their own mountain (John 4:20) and kept their own copy of the books of Moses; Jews and Samaritans usually kept apart. ‘The ends of the earth’ meant everyone else. The disciples were men from Galilee, a small region in the north. Now they were told the whole world was their field.

‘Witnesses’ is a word from the courtroom. A witness says what he has seen and heard. That is all Jesus asks of them. In this book it will cost Stephen his life (7:58-60), and James the brother of John his (12:2).
passages.ot:
Behind the promise of the Spirit stand Israel's prophets. Joel had said that God would one day pour out his Spirit on all people (Joel 2:28), and Peter will quote those words in the next chapter. Ezekiel had heard God promise, “I will put My Spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:27).

‘The ends of the earth’ is the prophets' phrase too. God says to his servant in Isaiah, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). In the same verse the servant's first task is “to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the protected ones of Israel”. Restoring Israel and reaching the nations belong together in Isaiah, and they belong together in Jesus' answer.
passages.hard:
What did the disciples mean by ‘restore the kingdom to Israel’, and what did Jesus' answer mean? Christians have read it in more than one way.

Many read it like this. The disciples were still thinking of an earthly kingdom for their nation. Jesus gently turns them to something larger: the kingdom comes now through the Spirit and the good news going to every nation. On this view Israel's hope is fulfilled in Jesus, the risen King, and in the people he gathers from Israel and from all the nations.

Others point out that Jesus does not say the hope is wrong. He only says the timing is not theirs to know. They connect this with other passages, such as Peter's promise of ‘the restoration of all things’ (3:21) and Paul's words that “all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:26), and they expect God still to keep a promise to the Jewish people in the future.

Many hold something of both. These notes do not settle the question. And none of these readings is a claim about any modern nation or its politics. The passage is about God's kingdom and God's timing, and these notes make no claim about any state of our day.
passages.asks: The disciples wanted a date. Jesus gave them a job. Ask which questions about the future take up your attention, and whether they keep you from what is plainly yours to do now. Notice too what Jesus promised: not that they would be strong enough, but that power would come to them. The task was too big for them, and it was meant to be.

passages.happening:
“After He had said this, they watched as He was taken up, and a cloud hid Him from their sight” (verse 9).

While they stand staring into the sky, two men dressed in white are suddenly beside them. “Men of Galilee,” they say, “why do you stand here looking into the sky? This same Jesus, who has been taken from you into heaven, will come back in the same way you have seen Him go into heaven” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Luke tells this moment twice, briefly at the end of his Gospel and more fully here. The two men in white remind the reader of the two men in shining clothes at the empty tomb (Luke 24:4). Once again heavenly messengers explain what the disciples cannot.

A cloud in Israel's story often meant God's own presence. A cloud went before Israel in the wilderness, and a cloud filled the temple. On the mountain where Jesus was transfigured, a cloud came over them and God spoke (Luke 9:34-35). So the cloud does not mean Jesus disappeared into the weather. It means he went into the presence of God.

This is what Christians call the ascension. The creeds say he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father. It does not mean Jesus is far away or retired. It means he has gone to the place of all authority, and from there, as Peter will soon say, he pours out the Spirit (2:33).

The angels' words also point forward. The same Jesus, not a different one, will come back, and in the same way: in person, and seen.
passages.ot:
Daniel saw “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” to the Ancient of Days, and he was given a kingdom (Daniel 7:13-14). At his trial Jesus had used those words of himself (Mark 14:62). Here he goes up in a cloud; he will come again the same way.

Elijah was taken up too: “Elijah went up into heaven in a whirlwind” (2 Kings 2:11). His follower Elisha had asked for a double share of his spirit, and was told he would have it if he saw Elijah taken (2 Kings 2:9-10). Many readers notice the likeness. The disciples watch Jesus go, and in a few days they receive his Spirit.
passages.asks: The angels asked why the disciples were standing there looking up. There was work to do, and a promise to wait for. Ask whether your hope of Jesus' return makes you more useful on earth or less. Christian hope is not staring at the sky. It is getting on with the work, knowing who is coming back.

passages.t: Back to the city, to pray
passages.happening:
They walk back to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, which Luke says was close by, “a Sabbath day’s journey away” (verse 12). They go to the upper room where they were staying.

Luke names the eleven: Peter and John, James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas son of James (verse 13).

“With one accord they all continued in prayer, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with His brothers” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
The Mount of Olives is the ridge just east of Jerusalem, across the Kidron valley. The distance in verse 12 was the farthest Jewish teaching allowed a person to walk on the Sabbath, about two thousand cubits, a little over half a mile or about one kilometre. The rule is set down later in the Mishnah, the collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, and it was linked to passages like Numbers 35:5. Luke's readers far away would not know the hill. Luke tells them it is a short walk.

The list of names is the list from Luke's Gospel (Luke 6:14-16), with one name gone: Judas Iscariot. Simon is called the Zealot. That may mean a man of fierce zeal for God's law, or someone who had belonged to a group that wanted to fight Rome; the Zealots as a named party belong to the war of 66 to 70, so many think the first meaning is likelier here.

Then come the women, who had followed Jesus from Galilee and stood near the cross and found the empty tomb. Mary, Jesus' mother, is named here for the last time in the Bible. And his brothers are there. During his ministry “even His own brothers did not believe in Him” (John 7:5). Paul says the risen Jesus appeared to one of them, James (1 Corinthians 15:7). Now they pray among his followers, and James will become a leader of the church in Jerusalem.

Christians have understood these ‘brothers’ in three ways: as later children of Mary and Joseph (the common Protestant view), as Joseph's children by an earlier marriage (the Orthodox view), or as cousins (a long Catholic view). The notes on Mark 3 and 6 say more.
passages.ot:
The pattern of waiting in prayer for God to act runs through Israel's Scriptures. The psalmist says, “Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous” (Psalm 27:14). Isaiah promises that “those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:31).

The Mount of Olives had its own place in the prophets. Ezekiel saw the glory of the Lord leave the city and stand “over the mountain east of the city” (Ezekiel 11:23), and Zechariah saw a day when the Lord's feet “will stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4). Some readers hear those words behind the angels' promise that Jesus will come back the same way. Luke does not draw the line himself.
passages.asks: After the most astonishing sight of their lives, the disciples did something ordinary. They went back to their room and prayed together, men and women, apostles and family, doubters who had come to believe. Ask who you pray with. The church was born in a prayer meeting before it was born in a sermon.

passages.happening:
A few days later Peter stands up among the believers, about a hundred and twenty people. He says that Scripture had to be fulfilled “concerning Judas, who became a guide for those who arrested Jesus. He was one of our number and shared in this ministry” (verses 16-17).

Luke then adds a note for his readers, in brackets. With the reward for his wickedness Judas bought a field, and there he fell headlong and his body burst open. Everyone in Jerusalem heard of it, and the field came to be called in their own language Akeldama, “that is, Field of Blood” (verse 19).

Peter quotes the book of Psalms: “May his place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in it,” and, “May another take his position” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Peter, who had denied Jesus three times, now leads. He does not hide from what Judas did, and he does not gloat. Judas was ‘one of our number’. The betrayer came from inside the circle. That is a sober thing for any group of believers to remember.

Akeldama is Aramaic, the everyday language of Jerusalem. Luke translates it for readers who spoke Greek. In the 300s the Christian writer Eusebius placed the field near the Hinnom valley, and Jerome after him placed it south of Mount Zion. The traditional site is where the Hinnom and Kidron valleys meet. Whether that is the true place cannot be known.

Notice how Peter reads the Psalms. Psalms 69 and 109 are prayers of a righteous man betrayed by those close to him. The first Christians read them as speaking of Jesus, the righteous sufferer, and of the one who betrayed him. Peter even changes one word to fit: the psalm says ‘their place’, and he says ‘his place’.
passages.ot:
The two lines come from Psalm 69:25, “May their place be deserted; let there be no one to dwell in their tents”, and Psalm 109:8, “May his days be few; may another take his position”.

Both are psalms of David that the New Testament reads often. Psalm 69 is quoted of Jesus in other places, for the vinegar given him to drink (Psalm 69:21) and his zeal for God's house (John 2:17). Peter reads the first line as the end of Judas and the second as a reason to fill his empty place among the Twelve.
passages.hard:
How did Judas die? Matthew says that he threw the silver into the temple “and hanged himself” (Matthew 27:5), and that the priests used the money to buy a potter's field, called the Field of Blood (Matthew 27:7-8). Acts says that Judas bought a field, fell headlong and burst open, and that the field was called Field of Blood. The two accounts are different, and honest readers have always noticed it.

Readers answer in more than one way. Since early times, many have joined the two: Judas hanged himself, and his body later fell, perhaps when the rope or branch gave way, and burst. The field was bought with his money, so it could be said that he bought it, even if the priests made the purchase. Others think the two writers handed on separate memories of his death, which agree on what matters most (a terrible death, a field bought with the price of betrayal, the name Field of Blood) but differ in the details, and they do not think the details need to be made to match. Either way, both writers tell Judas's end as the bitter fruit of his betrayal.

A word of care. Judas's death is told here in a few plain sentences. Many people carry shame for something they have done, and some have thought of ending their life. If that is you, please do not carry it alone. Tell God, and tell someone near you: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. If you have thought of ending your life, please reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service where you live. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Peter, who also failed Jesus, found mercy. These notes do not say what God did with Judas. That belongs to God.
passages.asks: The same night, two disciples failed Jesus. Peter denied him and Judas betrayed him. One wept and came back; the other despaired. Ask what you do with your own failures: whether you take them to the one who forgives, or carry them alone. And notice that Peter, forgiven, now speaks with care about the friend who fell.

passages.happening:
Peter says the gap must be filled. The new man must be one who was with them “the whole time the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from John’s baptism until the day Jesus was taken up from us” (verses 21-22). He must be a witness of the resurrection.

Two men are put forward: Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. The believers pray, “Lord, You know everyone’s heart. Show us which of these two You have chosen” (verse 24).

“Then they cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias; so he was added to the eleven apostles” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Why must there be twelve? Israel was made of twelve tribes, and Jesus had chosen twelve apostles as the start of God's renewed people. He had told them they would “sit on thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke 22:30). With Judas gone, the circle was broken. Before the Spirit comes and the message goes out to Israel, the Twelve are made whole again.

The choice was narrowed by plain tests first: a man who had walked with Jesus from the start and seen him risen. Then the believers prayed. Only then did they cast lots. Lots were marked objects that were cast, as Proverbs says, ‘into the lap’. In Israel this was a way of leaving a decision to God, not to chance. Priests were given their duties by lot, as Zechariah was (Luke 1:9).

This is the last time in the New Testament that believers choose by lot. After the Spirit comes, the church seeks God's leading by prayer, by the Spirit's guidance and by counsel together. Matthias is never mentioned again. Neither are most of the Twelve. The book is not about them, but about what the risen Jesus does through them.
passages.ot:
The custom comes from Israel's Scriptures. “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). The high priest carried the Urim and Thummim in his breastpiece, objects used to ask God's will (Exodus 28:30), and the land was shared out among the tribes by lot in the book of Joshua.

The prayer “You know everyone's heart” echoes what God told Samuel when he chose David: people look at the outward appearance, “but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).
passages.hard:
Was it right to choose by lot? Some readers think the apostles acted too quickly, and that God's real choice to fill the gap was Paul, called later by the risen Jesus himself. Most readers think Luke tells the story with approval: the believers prayed, Scripture guided them, and Luke says plainly that Matthias was “added to the eleven apostles”. Either way, the story is not given as a method for churches today. It happened once, before Pentecost.

And what of ‘his rightful place’ (verse 25), the place Judas went to? The words are spare, and readers have taken them in different ways. As at verse 18, these notes do not say what God did with Judas. That belongs to God.
passages.asks: They used their minds, they prayed, and then they trusted God with the outcome. Ask how you make large decisions: whether you do the thinking, whether you pray, and whether you can leave the result in God's hands. And notice the man who was not chosen. Joseph Barsabbas, called Justus, met every test and still was not picked. Faithfulness that is passed over is still seen by the one who knows every heart.
